A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, allowing reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original neural-network experiments on CIFAR-2, CIFAR-10, EuroSAT and Adult, including predictor distances, training durations and subgroup performance.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds AdamW results on imbalanced CIFAR-10 and incremental XGBoost results on Adult.

M1.justification: The majority/minority loss decomposition and analyzed gradient-flow/descent procedure remain unchanged. AdamW and XGBoost are additional experimental comparison methods, not newly proposed algorithms or components.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR-10, automobile/truck CIFAR-2, Highway/River EuroSAT and Adult income with the same subgroup tasks. The added optimizer and boosting experiments reuse existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 substantially broadens the evaluated learning methods beyond SGD-trained neural networks: Table 3 adds AdamW comparisons for five existing CIFAR-10 architectures, and Table 4 adds XGBoost alongside the Adult TabNet study. The original architecture comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The original reported settings and accuracy thresholds remain. Added experiments introduce AdamW with learning rate 1e-3, weight decay 1e-2 and cosine scheduling, plus incremental XGBoost training in batches of 10 trees with cumulative-time measurements. These supplement rather than replace the original protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained imbalance, architecture and initialization/stopping analyses, v2 explicitly tests whether minority-learning delay persists under adaptive optimization and outside neural networks. Appendices D.1 and E add substantive optimizer and model-family robustness checks using AdamW and XGBoost.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains means and standard deviations over 30 runs; Table 2 and the general reporting section retain three-seed averaging. The new AdamW table uses the same three-run averaging practice, without introducing a new uncertainty-estimation or statistical-testing procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds AdamW overcost results and XGBoost training/test trajectories in Tables 3–4. For example, AdamW ResNet18 reports overcosts of 465%, 342% and 209% across the three imbalance levels. Figure 2 replaces its curves and changes the reported unlucky-training duration from 800 to 600 epochs; equivalent runs are not established. Original Tables 1–2 and plotted data in Figures 3–8 remain.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 is reformulated on a subset K with new boundary-distance assumptions and revised proofs; separation and finiteness conclusions move into modified Corollary 2. V2 localizes the existing nonlinear duration lemma's Hessian bound to a ball containing the trajectory, and adds a dimensional volume claim and tightness/discrete-step derivations. The linear-regression results are retained in Appendix B.

C1.justification: The abstract's three central claims about predictor proximity, majority-dominated training and additional training duration remain. The introduction adds the contribution that delayed minority learning persists under AdamW and XGBoost, modestly broadening the claimed empirical reach.

C2.justification: V2 distinguishes short parameter-space travel from long training time, explicitly notes the impracticality of minority-aware stopping when groups are unknown, and qualifies larger-network recommendations with spurious-correlation risk. It also interprets the added experiments as demonstrating broader robustness, although the claimed XGBoost test-set catch-up is not supported by Table 4.

D1.justification: V1 promises a future code release; v2 Appendix F.5 states that code and configurations are available at a public repository. V2 also documents AdamW settings, XGBoost continuation in 10-tree batches, absence of SGD momentum, and the CIFAR-2/ResNet18 setting of Figure 2. Existing hardware, runtime and SGD hyperparameter disclosures remain.

R1.justification: V2 replaces much of the fairness-centered introduction with detailed positioning against earlier imbalance research. Its new related-literature discussion distinguishes its geometry and duration analysis from Anand et al., Francazi et al., and Gaussian/ridge analyses by Subramonian et al. and Mannelli et al. It also expands simplicity-bias and adaptive-optimization references while removing several general fairness citations.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction and contributions, adds a dedicated related-literature discussion, moves the main-text linear-regression case study into Appendix B, and reorganizes the proofs and gradient-training sections. It systematically renames fairness overcost as catch-up overcost and updates affiliation and conference-header text.

P2.justification: V2 adds AdamW/XGBoost Tables 3–4 and two compact analytical example tables, redraws Figure 2 and expands figure captions. Most existing displays retain their design and plotted content; the original runtime and hyperparameter tables become Tables 5–6. The overall visual format remains similar.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful comparisons, clearer research positioning, worked examples and stated code access. However, its new Theorem 1 condition (7) lower-bounds Hausdorff distance, which does not ensure the boundary clearance used in Appendix C.1's proof. Appendix E also claims test-set catch-up although Table 4 shows minority test accuracy remaining near 60%, versus roughly 87% for the majority. These new reliability problems coexist with substantive benefits, preventing a confident net quality judgment.
